latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: IgG autoantibody (and rarely IgM/IgA) binding ADAMTS13 spacer/CUB domains, neutralizing protease activity and accelerating clearance; underlies immune-mediated TTP (iTTP). In congenital TTP this mechanism is replaced by biallelic ADAMTS13 mutation but the downstream cascade is identical.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimer-platelet adhesion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endothelial-released ULvWF multimers, normally cleaved by ADAMTS13, persist on endothelium and bind platelet GPIbα, forming platelet-vWF microthrombi in the high-shear arteriolar/capillary microcirculation. Drives platelet consumption and microvascular obstruction.

Diffuse platelet-rich microthrombi occlude terminal arterioles and capillaries in brain, heart, kidney, mesentery, pancreas, and skin. Produces fluctuating neurologic deficits, troponin leak, mild AKI, abdominal pain, and contributes to LDH elevation through ischemic tissue release.

Erythrocytes traversing microthrombi-narrowed vessels are mechanically fragmented, generating schistocytes and intravascular hemolysis with LDH release, free hemoglobin, haptoglobin consumption, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Coombs-negative because mechanism is mechanical, not antibody-mediated.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Endothelial injury and feed-forward vWF release
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Microthrombosis and ischemia further damage endothelium, releasing additional ULvWF and propagating the cycle; also contributes to subtle DIC-like features (modest D-dimer elevation) without true consumptive coagulopathy.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Accumulated end-organ injury from treatment delay
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Each hour without plasma exchange in iTTP increases cumulative microthrombotic burden in CNS and myocardium. Defines short-term mortality risk and likelihood of permanent neurologic/cardiac sequelae. The clinical motto 'PLEX before confirmed ADAMTS13' reflects this.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Anti-ADAMTS13 IgG inhibitor neutralizes plasma ADAMTS13 protease activity; in iTTP measured activity is characteristically <10% (often <5% or undetectable).
Direct serologic reflection of the autoantibody-mediated mechanism; Bethesda assay quantifies functional inhibitor.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: active when adamts13_activity below ~10% of normal
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Without ADAMTS13 cleavage of vWF A2 domain, ULvWF multimers persist on endothelium and recruit platelets via GPIbα; threshold-like behavior near 10% activity.
ULvWF multimers detectable on multimer gel are the substrate of platelet adhesion in this disease.
Platelets are consumed in microvascular vWF-platelet aggregates; nadir typically 10–30 ×10^9/L, often <20.
Platelet-vWF aggregates physically occlude terminal arterioles, producing distributed micro-infarction.
RBCs are mechanically sheared as they traverse vessels narrowed by platelet-vWF microthrombi.
Ischemia-reperfusion injures endothelium, releasing more ULvWF and amplifying the cycle.
Damaged endothelium releases additional ULvWF stored in Weibel-Palade bodies, sustaining the thrombotic loop.
Mechanical RBC fragmentation produces helmet cells and schistocytes; threshold typically >1% (often 2–10%).
Intravascular hemolysis lowers hemoglobin; values commonly 7–10 g/dL at presentation.
Free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin which is then cleared; haptoglobin typically undetectable.
Heme catabolism produces unconjugated bilirubin; usually 2–5 mg/dL with normal liver enzymes.
Compensatory marrow erythroid response to hemolysis.
RBC lysis releases LDH; in TTP a substantial fraction also reflects ischemic tissue release, so LDH commonly 1000–3000 U/L (often disproportionate to anemia).
Ischemic tissue (kidney, heart, muscle) contributes additional LDH beyond hemolysis component; helps explain LDH-disproportionate-to-hemolysis pattern.
LDH-to-ULN ratio is a sensitive marker of ongoing hemolysis and is followed during PLEX response.
Mechanical (not antibody-mediated) hemolysis: DAT/Coombs is characteristically negative — a key discriminator from autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Evans syndrome.
Severe thrombocytopenia produces petechiae/purpura; mucosal bleeding less prominent than in ITP because consumption rather than failed production dominates.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: more pronounced when platelet_count below ~10 ×10^9/L or with procedures
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Major bleeding is uncommon at presentation despite very low platelet counts; thrombosis dominates the phenotype.
CNS microthrombi cause fluctuating confusion, headache, lethargy — most common neurologic manifestation, classically transient and waxing/waning.
Focal deficits (aphasia, hemiparesis, visual disturbance) from arteriolar microinfarcts; classically transient and migrating.
Cortical microthrombi can manifest as focal or generalized seizures.
Frequent early symptom from CNS microvascular involvement.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: typically mild rise; severe AKI should redirect toward complement-mediated TMA / Shiga toxin HUS
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Renal microthrombi commonly cause mild creatinine elevation (≤2 mg/dL); severe AKI is uncharacteristic of TTP.
Cardiac microthrombi produce troponin elevation in up to half of patients; correlates with mortality and is an independent predictor of poor outcome.
Subset of patients have angina-like chest pain from cardiac microthrombi.
Mesenteric or pancreatic microthrombi cause abdominal pain, occasionally with mild pancreatitis or ileus.
Low-grade fever (~37.5–38.5°C) is part of the classic pentad; high spiking fever should prompt re-evaluation for sepsis or HLH.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: mild-to-moderate elevation only; markedly elevated D-dimer with low fibrinogen and prolonged PT favors DIC
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Localized microvascular fibrin turnover causes modest D-dimer rise without consumptive coagulopathy.
Larger vessel occlusion or coalescing microthrombi can produce frank stroke; major contributor to early mortality and persistent neurologic disability.
Cardiac microthrombi can precipitate MI, arrhythmia, or sudden cardiac death; troponin elevation predicts this hazard.
Aggregate risk of any new thrombotic event during active disease.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: active when platelet_count <20 ×10^9/L, especially with concurrent ischemic stroke or after platelet transfusion
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Although thrombosis dominates, severe thrombocytopenia plus possible ischemic stroke confers ICH risk; inappropriate platelet transfusion can precipitate further microthrombosis or hemorrhage at infarct sites.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: rises sharply when platelet_count <10 ×10^9/L or with central line placement
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Major bleeding less common than expected for the thrombocytopenia degree, but procedure-related bleeding is meaningful.
Untreated iTTP carries ~90% mortality. PLEX initiated within 24 h reduces mortality to 10–20%. Each hour of delay adds CNS/cardiac micro-infarction.
Cardiac and cerebral microinfarction are the dominant proximate causes of TTP death.
Confirmed ADAMTS13 <10% with detectable inhibitor establishes iTTP diagnosis and supports rituximab consideration.
Compensatory marrow erythroid response to hemolysis.Same reticulocyte response represented in the alternate reporting form.
Immune TTP is commonly mediated by detectable anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody/inhibitor; positivity is a diagnostic-context finding, not a runtime label.
Hemolysis raises indirect bilirubin and can produce visible icterus/jaundice.
AST can rise with hemolysis in addition to ischemic tissue injury.
Microvascular ischemic tissue injury can raise AST.
Hepatic or systemic ischemic injury can mildly-moderately raise ALT.
Acute endothelial injury and systemic stress can produce leukocytosis in severe presentations.
Acute stress response and inflammatory triggers can increase neutrophils in severe presentations.

axes.shape_free_text: Healthy 50–150%; in active TTP <10% (often undetectable); rises gradually with PLEX/immunosuppression over weeks
Healthy undetectable; in iTTP typically 1–10 BU/mL at presentation; declines slowly with B-cell depletion (rituximab) over months
Healthy 150–400; nadir at presentation typically 10–30 (often <20); recovers to >150 within 3–10 days of effective PLEX/caplacizumab
Falls to 7–10 g/dL with active hemolysis; recovers over 1–4 weeks after disease control
Healthy <0.5%; TTP typically 2–10% on peripheral smear; clears over 1–3 weeks after disease control
Markedly elevated 1000–3000+ U/L (often >5× ULN), reflecting both hemolysis and ischemic tissue release; normalizes within 1–2 weeks of effective treatment
Often 3–10× ULN; followed daily during PLEX as a sensitive response marker
Suppressed/undetectable (<10 mg/dL) during active hemolysis; recovers slowly over 1–2 weeks
Indirect-predominant elevation 2–5 mg/dL with normal liver transaminases; normalizes over 1–2 weeks
Compensatory rise (often >100 ×10^9/L) emerging by day 3–7; normalizes after hemolysis resolves Range broadened to cover marked marrow response in severe microangiopathic hemolysis.
Characteristically negative throughout disease — key discriminator from autoimmune hemolytic anemia / Evans syndrome
Detectable on multimer gel during active disease; resolves with ADAMTS13 recovery
Mild elevation typical (1.0–2.0 mg/dL); severe AKI/dialysis dependence is uncharacteristic and should prompt aHUS / STEC-HUS reconsideration
Elevated in ~25–60% of patients reflecting cardiac microthrombi; independent predictor of mortality
Mild-to-moderate elevation (1–5 μg/mL FEU) from localized microvascular fibrin turnover; markedly higher values with low fibrinogen and prolonged PT favor DIC over TTP
Characteristically normal in TTP — key DIC discriminator
Characteristically normal in TTP
Normal or elevated (acute-phase) in TTP — key DIC discriminator
Confusion, lethargy, coma — fluctuating; present in 50–60% at presentation
Focal deficits — aphasia, hemiparesis, visual disturbance — classically transient and migrating
Less common; focal or generalized seizures in subset
Frequent early symptom
Common at presentation; reflects severity of thrombocytopenia
Mucosal bleeding less prominent than expected for the thrombocytopenia degree
Mesenteric/pancreatic microthrombosis; subset develop pancreatitis
Subset with cardiac involvement
Common nonspecific symptom from anemia and systemic illness
Low-grade fever (37.5–38.5°C) typical; high spiking fever should prompt sepsis/HLH evaluation
Mild tachycardia from anemia and systemic illness
Pre-test high (PLASMIC score 6–7); confirmed by ADAMTS13 <10% with detectable inhibitor
Depends on institutional apheresis availability and central line placement; lower in resource-limited settings
Elevated in IgA-deficient patients and prior plasma reactions; mitigated with washed/IgA-deficient FFP
Modulates caplacizumab use and timing of central line placement
Elevated by central line, plasma exposure, corticosteroids, and rituximab
Relevant before rituximab; HBsAg/anti-HBc screening required
Pregnancy is both a trigger and a treatment-modifying context (caplacizumab pregnancy data limited; rituximab generally avoided)
Recent viral infection (HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, gastroenteritis) precedes a notable subset of episodes
High during untreated phase, falls rapidly with PLEX + caplacizumab
Cardiac microthrombosis-driven; elevated troponin signals risk
Aggregate hazard for any new thrombotic event during active disease
Low overall; rises with severe thrombocytopenia, post-stroke hemorrhagic conversion, and inappropriate platelet transfusion
Modest at baseline (consumption pattern); rises with caplacizumab and procedures
Concentrated around central line placement; mitigated by ultrasound-guided femoral access and careful timing
Untreated iTTP ~90% mortality; with timely PLEX + immunosuppression ± caplacizumab overall mortality 10–20%; cardiac/CNS microthrombosis dominate causes of death

Reticulocyte percentage; separate from absolute reticulocyte count because percent and 10^9/L are not interchangeable without RBC count. Range broadened to cover marked marrow response in severe microangiopathic hemolysis.
Detectable anti-ADAMTS13 antibody/inhibitor supports immune TTP; separate finding from quantitative inhibitor titer.
Jaundice/icterus may accompany indirect hyperbilirubinemia from microangiopathic hemolysis.
AST may rise from hemolysis and ischemic tissue injury in active TTP.
ALT can be mildly-moderately elevated from hepatic ischemia or overlap inflammatory trigger; not a primary TTP discriminator.
Stress leukocytosis or trigger-associated inflammation may accompany acute TTP presentations.
Neutrophilia may reflect stress, tissue ischemia, corticosteroid exposure, or inflammatory trigger in acute TTP.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Daily PLEX response is judged by simultaneous platelet rise and LDH fall; tight inverse coupling beyond what is captured by individual mechanism edges.
Both move with hemolysis intensity; residual covariance after the common mechanism is partialed out.
Same-patient CNS microthrombi typically produce both global and focal manifestations together; classic fluctuating waxing/waning pattern.
Bedside skin findings track platelet nadir and recovery in real time.
Troponin elevation is an independent predictor of TTP mortality even after adjusting for other markers, reflecting cardiac micro-infarction load.
In iTTP these two move inversely under shared autoimmune drive; tracking both during follow-up helps detect impending relapse.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Without apheresis access bridging therapy with FFP infusion is used until transfer; suboptimal.
Reactions interrupt sessions; mitigated with antihistamine/steroid premedication or IgA-deficient plasma.
Should be initiated empirically on high pre-test probability (PLASMIC ≥6) without waiting for ADAMTS13 result.

side_effects.interpretation: Citrate-induced hypocalcemia; perioral paresthesias; replace IV calcium
Catheter-related bloodstream infection; bacteremia risk increases with prolonged access
Central line placement in severely thrombocytopenic patient

treatments.context_specific_role: Initiated emergently within 4–8 hours of clinical suspicion (PLASMIC ≥6); 1.0–1.5 plasma volume daily until platelet >150 ×10^9/L for 2 consecutive days, then taper.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage contraindicates caplacizumab.
Triple therapy (PLEX + steroids + caplacizumab) reduces refractory disease, exacerbations, and time to platelet recovery (HERCULES, TITAN).

side_effects.interpretation: Mucocutaneous bleeding, epistaxis, gingival bleeding common
Major bleeding rare but reported; hold around invasive procedures

treatments.context_specific_role: Daily SC injection alongside PLEX + immunosuppression; continued ≥30 days post-PLEX cessation, extended if ADAMTS13 not recovered to avoid rebound.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Suppresses autoreactive B/T cells producing anti-ADAMTS13.
Worsens infectious risk in already-immunocompromised host.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct to PLEX from day 1; high-dose pulse (methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 3 days) often used in severe disease, then tapered.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Mandatory HBV screening; entecavir/tenofovir prophylaxis if HBcAb+ to prevent fulminant reactivation.
Generally avoided in pregnancy due to neonatal B-cell depletion; case-specific.

side_effects.interpretation: B-cell depletion 6–12 months; respiratory infections, HBV reactivation

treatments.context_specific_role: Front-loaded in severe iTTP, refractory disease, exacerbation, or relapse; pre-emptive use during ADAMTS13 relapse (activity dropping <10% before clinical recurrence) is increasingly standard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Definitive for congenital TTP (cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman); in iTTP, anti-ADAMTS13 antibody can neutralize it, limiting effect.
High inhibitor titers reduce efficacy in iTTP.

side_effects.interpretation: Generally well tolerated; infusion reactions uncommon

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard prophylaxis and on-demand for cTTP; emerging investigational role in refractory iTTP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Used only when PLEX cannot be initiated within hours; provides ADAMTS13 but cannot remove inhibitor.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporary bridge until apheresis available; clearly inferior to PLEX and never substituted for it long-term.
Supports erythropoiesis during sustained hemolysis; routine adjunct.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Platelet transfusion historically associated with worsening microthrombosis; reserved strictly for life-threatening bleeding (e.g., ICH) or as cover for emergent procedures.

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard supportive principle; communicated explicitly to ED/ICU teams to avoid reflexive transfusion at low platelet thresholds.
Rescue/maintenance for refractory iTTP, rituximab failure, or as steroid-sparing agent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removes major site of antibody production and platelet sequestration in selected refractory iTTP.

side_effects.interpretation: Lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (encapsulated organisms)

treatments.context_specific_role: Rare in modern era; reserved for chronic refractory/relapsing iTTP failing rituximab and other immunosuppression.

african_ancestry.trajectory_modulation: Higher iTTP incidence and possibly higher relapse rate; HLA-DRB1*11 associated

30_to_50_years.trajectory_modulation: Peak incidence of iTTP in this band

pregnant_or_postpartum.trajectory_modulation: Trigger event; physiologic ADAMTS13 fall in 2nd/3rd trimester unmasks cTTP and precipitates iTTP; HELLP/preeclampsia is a major mimicker

hiv_positive.trajectory_modulation: Strong trigger; ART suppression reduces incidence

active_sle.trajectory_modulation: iTTP can present concurrently with SLE flare; consider as part of overlap autoimmunity

risk_factors.factor: Drug exposure (ticlopidine, clopidogrel, quinine, gemcitabine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mitomycin, bevacizumab, interferon)

implicated_drug_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Drug-induced TMA — ADAMTS13 may be normal/mildly low (toxic mechanism distinct from iTTP); supports drug withdrawal as primary management

risk_factors.factor: Recent infection (gastroenteritis, viral URI, COVID-19, influenza)

recent_infection.trajectory_modulation: Common antecedent trigger of iTTP episodes

high_bmi.trajectory_modulation: Independent risk factor and possible relapse predictor

risk_factors.factor: Allogeneic HSCT or solid organ transplant

post_transplant.trajectory_modulation: Calcineurin inhibitor-associated TMA / transplant-associated TMA — overlapping phenotype with TTP but distinct mechanism (often complement-mediated)

homozygous_or_compound_heterozygous.trajectory_modulation: Defines congenital TTP (cTTP); presents in neonates/children or unmasked in pregnancy/adulthood; no inhibitor; treated with prophylactic FFP or recombinant ADAMTS13 rather than rituximab

prior_ittp.trajectory_modulation: Lifetime relapse risk 30–50%; ADAMTS13 surveillance every 3–6 months guides pre-emptive rituximab

active_malignancy.trajectory_modulation: Cancer-associated TMA overlaps with TTP differential; chemotherapy agents and disseminated mucin-producing adenocarcinoma can mimic

present.trajectory_modulation: SLE is a recognized autoimmune background/trigger for acquired immune TTP and can add fever, CRP, renal, and neurologic complexity.

supportive_care: Daily monitoring of platelet count, LDH, hemoglobin, schistocytes, creatinine, and troponin during PLEX therapy
Folate supplementation (5 mg PO daily) during sustained hemolysis
Avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding or as cover for absolutely necessary invasive procedure
Cardiac monitoring (telemetry, baseline troponin, ECG) given high prevalence of cardiac microthrombosis
Neurologic monitoring with periodic NIHSS-style focused exam to detect new deficits early
Ultrasound-guided femoral or jugular central line for PLEX (avoid subclavian to allow direct compression if bleeding)
IV calcium replacement during PLEX to counter citrate-induced hypocalcemia
DVT prophylaxis with mechanical compression initially; pharmacologic prophylaxis once platelet count >50 ×10^9/L
PPI for stress ulcer prophylaxis and steroid co-administration
HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc) and TB screening before rituximab; antiviral prophylaxis if anti-HBc positive
Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) during prolonged corticosteroid + rituximab therapy
Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and H. influenzae type b vaccination at least 2 weeks before splenectomy if performed
Transition planning with hematology for ADAMTS13 surveillance every 3–6 months for relapse prevention; pre-emptive rituximab if ADAMTS13 falls <10–20%
Genetic testing for ADAMTS13 mutations if ADAMTS13 persistently low without detectable inhibitor or in pediatric/familial presentations
Counseling on relapse warning signs (fatigue, bruising, headache) and clear ED return plan
Pregnancy counseling — high risk of relapse; close hematologic and obstetric co-management with serial ADAMTS13 monitoring
Psychological support and cognitive screening for post-TTP cognitive sequelae, depression, and PTSD which are common after recovery
